newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo lifts loss estimate, blames Hamanaka.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo lifts loss estimate, blames Hamanaka.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp on Thursday raised its estimated loss from unauthorised copper trading to $2.6 billion from the $1.8 billion announced June 13 and said it would press criminal charges against dismissed copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, whom it blamed for the debacle.

The higher copper loss, attributed to a drop in copper prices in mid-June as Sumitomo was seeking to liquidate unauthorised long positions, forced the trading giant to revise its 1996/97 group earnings forecast to a 147 billion yen ($1.34 billion) loss from a profit of 24 billion yen ($220 million).
Sumitomo President Kenji Miyahara told a press conference that most of the off-the-books positions had now been liquidated and it did not expect any further revisions to the estimates.

Traders said the news had little immediate effect on the copper market, however, with London Metal Exchange benchmark three-month copper hovering around the prior session's close of $1,920 a tonne at 1200 GMT, off from an earlier high of $1,953.

Sumitomo management said that, according to an on-going in-house probe, a 6.5 billion yen off-the-books loss Hamanaka made around 1985 eventually snowballed more than 40-fold to the latest estimate of 285 billion yen, as he tried to win back the losses with massive and multiple unauthorised trades.
Miyahara said Hamanaka conducted as many as 2,000 unauthorised deals on the LME in a single year and accused him of forging or doctoring documents to cover his tracks.
Miyahara also said that a 60-strong task force is still sifting through 2,000 cardboard boxes full of documents and that it would take time for all the details to emerge.
He declined to comment on whether Hamanaka had cooperated with the company's investigation.
"What we want to prove most at the moment is that the company was not involved with Hamanaka's unauthorised copper trading," he said.

He also said that Hamanaka's positions were closed out after the company's June 13 announcement, denying charges that some liquidation was carried out before the losses were made public. The liquidation was conducted in consultation with overseas regulators, he said.
He added that it had taken some time to liquidate the positions as the market was highly sensitive to Sumitomo's activities.

In the week-and-a-half following Sumitomo's June 13 announcement, the price of benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange fell nearly 20 percent to a 2-1/2-year low of $1,745 a tonne. The market managed a modest recovery and in recent months has held mostly to an $1,850 to $2,000 range. --Tokyo Commodities Desk (81-3 3432 6179)
